stem: In earlier times, what did people call a group of stars that appeared to form a pattern in the sky?
options: A constellation
A galaxy
An asteroid belt
A solar system
explanation: Correct option: (A). Groups of stars forming patterns were called constellations. A galaxy has millions to billions of stars, the asteroid belt is a region of rocky objects between Mars and Jupiter, and a solar system is a star with the objects that revolve around it.

stem: Which star is the brightest star in the night sky?
options: The Pole Star
Betelgeuse
Sirius
Aldebaran
explanation: Correct option: (C). Sirius, in the constellation Canis Major, is the brightest star in the night sky. The Pole Star is not very bright, while Betelgeuse (in Orion) and Aldebaran (in Taurus) are bright but less bright than Sirius.

stem: Long before the magnetic compass was invented, sailors and travellers learnt to recognise star patterns. What was the main use of this skill for them?
options: Predicting the rainfall of the season
Measuring how deep the sea was
Working out how big each star was
Finding directions at sea or on land
explanation: Correct option: (D). Recognising stars and their patterns helped sailors and travellers find directions, and it is still used as a backup method in emergencies. Star patterns do not tell rainfall, sea depth or the actual size of stars.

stem: A student has found the three bright stars in a short straight line in the middle of Orion. How can she now find Sirius?
options: Follow the line of the three stars towards the west
Follow the line of the three stars towards the east
Extend a line from the end stars of the Big Dipper
Look for the faintest star directly above Orion
explanation: Correct option: (B). The three middle stars form the hunter's belt. Imagining a straight line through them and looking along it towards the east leads to Sirius, which is close to Orion. Going west leads away from it, the Big Dipper's end stars are used to find the Pole Star, and Sirius is very bright, not faint.

stem: In Indian astronomy, Ardra is the star Betelgeuse in Orion, and Krittika is the group of stars called the Pleiades in Taurus. Which conclusion follows from these two examples?
options: A nakshatra may be one star or a group of stars
A nakshatra is always a single bright star
Ardra and Krittika lie in the same constellation
A nakshatra is one of the 88 regions set by the IAU
explanation: Correct option: (A). Ardra is a single star while Krittika is a group of stars, so a nakshatra can denote either. Krittika alone already rules out 'always a single star'; Ardra is in Orion and Krittika in Taurus, so they are in different constellations; and the 88 regions are the IAU constellations, not the nakshatras.

stem: To find the Pole Star, you imagine a line through the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup and extend it towards the north. About how far along this line is the Pole Star?
options: About twice the gap between those two stars
About ten times the gap between those two stars
Exactly at the brightest star found along that line
About five times the gap between those two stars
explanation: Correct option: (D). At about five times the distance between the two end stars of the cup, the line leads to a star that is not very bright: the Pole Star. Twice or ten times that gap would miss it, and the Pole Star is not the brightest star along the line.

stem: Yangdol sees thousands of stars at night in Nubra, but her cousin in a big city sees only a few. What is the most likely reason?
options: The city sky has more artificial light, smoke and dust
Fewer stars exist above big cities than above villages
Stars shine only above high mountain regions
City nights are shorter, so stars have less time to appear
explanation: Correct option: (A). The number of stars does not depend on where you stand; stars in cities are hidden by light pollution, smoke and dust, while Nubra has almost no air or light pollution. Stars do not shine only over mountains, and the length of the night does not explain the difference.

stem: Read the case about Dorjay's plan. Which change would most improve his chances of spotting the Pole Star?
options: Choose a full-moon night so that the sky is brighter
Choose a moonless, cloudless night and let his eyes adjust
Watch from the lit terrace so that the house lights guide him
Start looking at once, before his eyes get used to dark
explanation: Correct option: (B). The Pole Star is not very bright, so a night with neither the Moon nor clouds is best, and waiting about half an hour lets the eyes adjust to darkness. A full Moon and house lights brighten the sky and hide faint stars, and looking at once gives the eyes no time to adjust.

stem: Stars shine both day and night, yet we cannot see them during the day. Why?
options: Stars stop giving out light in daytime
Stars move below the Earth every morning
Clouds cover all the stars every day
The Sun's extreme brightness hides them

stem: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 269000 au away. Which statement correctly interprets this figure?
options: It is about 269000 km away from the Earth
It is about 269000 times as far from us as the Sun
It is about 269000 times bigger than the Sun
Its light takes about 269000 days to travel to the Earth
explanation: Correct option: (B). One au is about the Earth-Sun distance, so 269000 au means about 269000 times our distance to the Sun (roughly 269000 x 150 million km). The au measures distance, not size or time, and it is far larger than a kilometre.

stem: Pluto revolves around the Sun, yet it is no longer counted as a planet. Why?
options: Pluto stopped revolving around the Sun
Pluto was found to be a moon of Neptune
Pluto was found to be a bright star
The IAU redefined planets in 2006
explanation: Correct option: (D). When more small objects like Pluto were found, the International Astronomical Union in 2006 redefined what a planet is, and Pluto became a dwarf planet. Pluto still revolves around the Sun, it is not Neptune's moon, and it is not a star.

stem: Venus is farther from the Sun than Mercury, yet Venus is hotter. Which reason explains this?
options: Venus produces its own heat and light
Venus has an atmosphere that traps heat
Venus is bigger than the Sun itself
Venus is closer to the Earth than Mercury
explanation: Correct option: (B). Planets get most of their energy from the Sun, but an atmosphere can trap heat and change a planet's temperature a lot; this is why Venus is hotter than Mercury. Planets do not produce their own light, Venus is far smaller than the Sun, and nearness to Earth does not affect its temperature.

stem: Just after sunset, a student sees two bright dots near the western sky. One twinkles a lot; the other shines steadily and is very bright. What is the best conclusion?
options: The steady one is likely Venus; the other is likely a star
The twinkling one is likely Venus; the other is a star
Both must be stars, as planets are never seen without a telescope
Both must be planets, as stars twinkle only at dawn
explanation: Correct option: (A). Stars appear to twinkle a lot, unlike planets, and Venus, the brightest object after the Sun and the Moon, is seen near the West after sunset. So the steady, very bright dot is likely Venus. Venus, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can be seen with the naked eye, and stars twinkle at any time of night.

stem: Craters on the Moon's surface remain unchanged for a very long time. Which reason best explains this?
options: The Moon takes about 27 days to go once around the Earth
The Moon is about a quarter of the Earth's size
The Moon has no air, water or life to wear them away
The Moon produces its own light and heat

stem: Why does a comet develop a long tail as it comes close to the Sun?
options: Its frozen material starts to evaporate
It catches fire from rubbing against air
It collides with asteroids on its way
It reflects the light of distant stars
explanation: Correct option: (A). Comets are made of dust, gases, rocks and ice. Near the Sun the frozen material evaporates, and this evaporating material forms the tail. stem: Apart from the Sun, objects of the Solar System such as planets and the Moon are seen shining. Why?
options: They produce their own heat and their own light
They reflect sunlight from their surfaces
They burn gases in their atmospheres
They absorb light from the Milky Way

stem: The search for life beyond the Earth has mostly been directed towards exoplanets. What are exoplanets?
options: Dwarf planets that are found beyond the orbit of Neptune
Moons that revolve around the giant planets
Planets revolving around stars other than the Sun
Planets seen only with the help of a telescope
explanation: Correct option: (C). Exoplanets are planets discovered revolving around other stars in our galaxy. Dwarf planets such as Pluto and the moons of giant planets belong to our Solar System, and being seen with a telescope does not make a planet an exoplanet.

stem: From a dark spot in Ladakh on a moonless night, Dorjay sees a faint band of light running from near north to south across the sky. His friend in a brightly lit city cannot see it. Which explanation fits both facts?
options: It is a comet's tail, seen only from mountains
It is the asteroid belt, seen only from high places
It is a long thin cloud that the heat of cities clears away
It is our galaxy, and city lights hide its faint glow
explanation: Correct option: (D). The faint band is the Milky Way Galaxy, made of a huge number of stars. Its light is faint, so it is seen only from dark places, away from city lights and light pollution. A comet's tail, the asteroid belt or a cloud do not form this band.
